defaults.permitted_development: Across County County Durham, householder boundary works are normally allowed without a planning application up to 2 metres in height, dropping to 1 metre beside a highway used by vehicles or its footpath. Those usual limits do not override listed-building controls or any local condition that removes permitted development rights.

rules.height_rules: Across County County Durham, the usual boundary limits are 2 metres overall, or 1 metre where the enclosure sits next to a highway used by vehicles. A site that has been raised, terraced or fronted by a retaining wall can reach those limits faster than homeowners expect.
rules.depth_rules: Across County County Durham, depth is not usually the deciding measurement for fences and walls. The issue is more often whether the enclosure follows the normal boundary line or turns into a more substantial engineered structure with level changes behind it.
rules.boundary_rules: Across County County Durham, the enclosure may be permitted development on height, but still problematic on boundary position. Corner plots, access points, neighbouring listed curtilage and conservation-area demolition controls are all common complications.
rules.roof_rules: Across County County Durham, a fence or wall is not judged on roof form, but the top treatment still matters. Copings, trellis panels, archways and taller gate piers can all change the effective height and appearance.
rules.materials_rules: Across County County Durham, there is no blanket requirement to copy the house materials, although front boundaries generally work better when the walling, railings or panels feel in scale with the street rather than engineered or overbearing.

Those usual limits do not override listed-building controls or any local condition that removes permitted development rights.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: If the property is listed, or the boundary adjoins listed curtilage structures, changing the enclosure can need listed building consent as well as planning review.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: In Darlington, a new fence, wall or gate at a house is usually permitted development up to 2 metres high, or up to 1 metre where it is next to a highway used by vehicles or the footpath of such a highway. The normal right falls away where listed-building controls, Article 4 directions or relevant planning conditions apply.

rules.height_rules: Height is the first check for fences and walls: 2 metres is the normal cap, reduced to 1 metre beside a highway used by vehicles or its footpath. Be careful with sloping ground or built-up levels, because the measurement is taken from ground level and not from the top of a bank.
rules.depth_rules: Boundary enclosures do not have a national depth rule. The more useful checks are where the line sits, whether it encroaches visually on the frontage, and whether it also acts as a retaining wall.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary works that sit by a driveway, corner plot or junction still need safe visibility. The normal right is also restricted if the boundary adjoins a listed building or its curtilage, and demolition controls can matter in conservation areas.
rules.roof_rules: Fences and walls do not have a roof test, but cappings, trellis toppers, pergola-style additions or gates fixed to taller piers can all count toward the overall height and visual impact. Keep the whole boundary composition in mind rather than only the main panel height.
rules.materials_rules: Material choice is not controlled in the same way as height, yet it still matters. A boundary that fits the character of the house and street will usually sit more comfortably than one with overly heavy or visually harsh materials on a prominent frontage.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: Boundary works to or around a listed building can require listed building consent, especially where historic walls, railings, piers or gates are being altered or removed.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.
